6.about: A set of eighteen short pieces alternately signed with the initials of Schumann’s two invented alter egos, the impetuous Florestan and the gentle Eusebius, embodying an imaginary ’League of David’ (Davidsbund) that Schumann conceived as a band of artistic idealists fighting philistinism in music and culture.
6.ctx: Composed in 1837, the year Schumann and Clara Wieck secretly became engaged despite her father’s continued opposition, the piece is saturated with private, coded references to Clara, including a motto theme Schumann said was hers.
facts: Its pieces are individually signed with the initials of Schumann’s invented alter egos, Florestan and Eusebius.
Composed the year Schumann and Clara Wieck secretly became engaged.
Its opening theme is, by Schumann’s own account, based on a melody of Clara’s.

9.about: A masked-ball fantasy of twenty short, contrasting pieces, each a musical portrait of a real or invented character — including Chopin and Paganini, and Schumann’s own two imagined alter egos, the fiery Florestan and the dreamy Eusebius — built throughout on a four-note musical cipher derived from the letters of the Bohemian town Asch, spelling out a code connecting the piece to Schumann’s then-fiancée Ernestine von Fricken, who was from there.
9.ctx: Composed in 1834–35, in the turbulent period of Schumann’s brief engagement to Ernestine von Fricken before his affections turned decisively to Clara Wieck, the piece reflects the imaginative, literary sensibility Schumann brought to piano composition, treating the keyboard as a stage for characters and ideas rather than pure abstract form.
parts: A portrait in the style of Chopin’s own nocturnes.
A whirlwind portrait of the virtuoso violinist.
facts: Built throughout on a musical cipher spelling the name of a Bohemian town connected to Schumann’s fiancée at the time.
Includes musical portraits of Chopin, Paganini, and Schumann’s own two invented alter egos.
One of the most imaginatively literary works in the piano repertoire.

13.about: A set of variations of enormous scope and difficulty on a theme supplied by the amateur flautist Baron von Fricken, father of Schumann’s then-fiancée Ernestine, transforming a modest theme into a series of increasingly virtuosic ’symphonic’ études that push toward the scale and grandeur of orchestral writing on a solo instrument.
13.ctx: Composed between 1834 and 1837 and substantially revised in 1852, the work reflects Schumann’s ambition to expand the theme-and-variation form to symphonic scale and drama, incorporating, in its finale, a theme borrowed from an opera by Heinrich Marschner as tribute to a friend.
facts: Based on a theme supplied by the father of Schumann’s one-time fiancée.
Substantially revised by Schumann fifteen years after its first publication.
Among the most technically demanding works in Schumann’s output.

16.about: A set of eight fantasy pieces named after Johannes Kreisler, an eccentric, half-mad fictional musician invented by the writer E. T. A. Hoffmann, alternating stormy, agitated movements with passages of tender lyricism, reflecting the dual personality — the fiery Florestan and the dreamy Eusebius — that Schumann projected onto much of his music.
16.ctx: Composed in 1838 while Schumann was in Vienna attempting, unsuccessfully, to establish a music journal there, and while his relationship with Clara Wieck remained bitterly opposed by her father; Schumann dedicated the work to Chopin, who reportedly found it strange but interesting.
facts: Named after a fictional, half-mad musician invented by the writer E. T. A. Hoffmann.
Dedicated to Chopin.
Composed during a period of intense personal turmoil over Clara Wieck.

38.about: Nicknamed the ’Spring’ Symphony, Schumann’s first completed symphony, composed in a burst of creative energy in the early months of his marriage to Clara, its bright, optimistic character reportedly inspired by a poem evoking the arrival of spring.
38.ctx: Composed in just four days of sketching in January 1841, the first full year of Schumann’s marriage to Clara, a period of intense happiness and creative productivity that also produced much of his celebrated song output the previous year; Mendelssohn conducted the premiere.
parts: Andante un poco maestoso — Allegro molto vivace
A festive movement inspired, Schumann said, by the arrival of spring.
facts: Schumann’s first completed symphony.
Sketched in just four days.
Premiered under the direction of Mendelssohn.

44.about: One of the great works of the chamber repertoire, composed in a single extraordinarily productive year Schumann devoted almost entirely to chamber music, its slow movement, a funeral march, framed by outer movements of exuberant, symphonic energy unusual for a work involving piano and only four strings.
44.ctx: Composed in 1842, during what Schumann himself called his ’chamber music year’, following his intensive study of Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven’s chamber works; Clara Schumann, ill at the time of the planned premiere, was replaced at the piano by Felix Mendelssohn, who sight-read the demanding part.
parts: In modo d’una marcia: Un poco largamente
A vigorous finale ending in a fugue.
facts: Composed during what Schumann called his ’chamber music year’.
Mendelssohn sight-read the piano part at the private premiere when Clara Schumann fell ill.
Its finale closes with a fugal passage combining themes from the first and last movements.

48.about: A cycle of sixteen songs setting poems by Heinrich Heine tracing the arc of a love affair from infatuation through betrayal to resigned grief, ending with a long piano postlude that some scholars hear as summarizing, wordlessly, everything the songs themselves could not fully express.
48.ctx: Composed in 1840, the year Schumann finally married Clara after years of opposition from her father and a court battle to secure the right to marry — a year so overflowing with song composition that it is often called his ’year of song’, during which he wrote well over a hundred songs.
facts: Composed during 1840, Schumann’s prolific ’year of song’, the year he finally married Clara.
Sets sixteen poems by Heinrich Heine.
Ends with an extended piano postlude many hear as the cycle’s true emotional summary.

54.about: Schumann’s only piano concerto and one of the most beloved in the Romantic repertoire, growing out of a single-movement Fantasy for piano and orchestra Schumann wrote in 1841, to which he later added two further movements at the urging of his wife Clara, herself a celebrated concert pianist, who premiered the completed work.
54.ctx: Composed in two stages — the opening movement in 1841, the remaining two in 1845 — the concerto treats piano and orchestra as genuine partners rather than showcasing the soloist alone, a quality Clara Schumann, who championed the work throughout her long performing career, particularly prized.
parts: An urgent opening movement, originally conceived as a standalone Fantasy.
facts: Began life in 1841 as a standalone one-movement Fantasy before two further movements were added.
Premiered by Schumann’s wife, the celebrated pianist Clara Schumann.
Schumann’s only completed piano concerto.

97.about: Nicknamed the ’Rhenish’ Symphony for its evocation of life along the Rhine River, where Schumann had recently settled as municipal music director; its stately fourth movement was reportedly inspired by the ceremonial grandeur of Cologne Cathedral, which Schumann had visited during the elevation of a local archbishop to cardinal.
97.ctx: Composed in 1850, shortly after Schumann took up his post in Düsseldorf, a position that initially brought him and Clara considerable happiness, before the symptoms of the mental illness that would eventually institutionalize him began to worsen in the years that followed.
parts: A solemn movement inspired by Cologne Cathedral.
facts: Its fourth movement was inspired by the ceremony and architecture of Cologne Cathedral.
Composed shortly after Schumann became municipal music director in Düsseldorf.
Has five movements rather than the usual four.

15/7.about: Titled ’Reverie’, the seventh and by far the most famous of the thirteen pieces of Kinderszenen (’Scenes from Childhood’), a brief, tender miniature built on a simple, songlike melody that has become one of the most widely recognized pieces of piano music ever written.
15/7.ctx: Composed in 1838 as part of Kinderszenen, which Schumann described not as music written for children but as an adult’s affectionate, retrospective recollection of childhood, written during the years of his passionate courtship of Clara Wieck, whom he would marry two years later after overcoming her father’s fierce opposition.
facts: The most famous of the thirteen pieces of Kinderszenen.
Schumann described the set as an adult’s memory of childhood, not music for children to play.
Composed during his courtship of Clara Wieck.

68/10.about: Titled ’The Happy Farmer, Returning from Work’, one of the best-known pieces ever written for beginning pianists, a bright, cheerful miniature that has introduced generations of students to Schumann’s music.
68/10.ctx: Composed in 1848 as part of the Album for the Young, a collection Schumann wrote for his own children, graded roughly in order of difficulty from simple beginner pieces to more demanding ones, reflecting his deep interest, shared with Clara, in music education.
facts: One of the most widely taught beginner piano pieces ever written.
Part of the Album for the Young, composed for Schumann’s own children.
Its full title translates as ’The Happy Farmer, Returning from Work’.

82/7.about: Titled ’Bird as Prophet’, an atmospheric, harmonically unusual miniature from the forest-themed suite Waldszenen, its hesitant, unpredictable melody suggesting birdsong more through gesture and silence than direct imitation.
82/7.ctx: Composed in 1848–49 as part of Waldszenen (’Forest Scenes’), a suite of nine character pieces evoking different aspects of a walk through the woods, from hunters and flowers to, in this piece, an eerie encounter with a bird imagined as an oracle.
facts: Part of the nine-piece suite Waldszenen (’Forest Scenes’).
One of the most harmonically adventurous of Schumann’s shorter character pieces.
Its unpredictable, hesitant melody suggests birdsong without directly imitating it.
